question: You want Claude Code to explore an unfamiliar repository with zero risk of it changing files or running destructive commands. Which permission mode is designed for exactly this?
options: Accept-edits mode, which shows every proposed edit for review without ever applying it
Plan mode, which restricts Claude to read-only exploration — it can search and read, but not mutate anything
Bypass-permissions mode, which routes every action through an extra safety check first
Default mode after running /clear, so there is no accumulated context to act on
explanation: Plan mode is the harness's read-only dial: Claude can roam the codebase — searching, reading, building an understanding — but the harness withholds the mutating tools, so nothing can be edited or destructively executed. That's what makes it the safe way to let the agent explore unfamiliar code. The other modes point the opposite direction: accept-edits auto-approves file edits (it reduces prompting, it doesn't prevent changes), and bypass-permissions skips prompting entirely — it's the least protective mode, meant for disposable environments like containers, not for caution. /clear is a context operation, not a permission one: it empties the conversation but changes nothing about what tools may run. Like all permission machinery, modes live in the harness on your machine, so they behave identically whether you're on Bedrock or the Anthropic API.

question: At a permission prompt, you pick the option to allow this command 'always' so you're never asked about it again. What did that choice actually do?
options: Set a temporary flag that lasts until you close the terminal window
Taught the model your preference, so it remembers it in future sessions
Turned off permission prompts entirely for this project going forward
Wrote a durable allow rule into a settings file, so future matching calls are pre-approved
explanation: Answering 'always' is rule-writing: the harness appends an allow rule for that command pattern to a settings file, and from then on the rule matches before any prompt is needed. That's why the choice survives restarting the terminal — it's on disk, not in session memory. It is not model memory: the model is stateless and never receives permission rules at all, so nothing was 'taught.' And it is far narrower than disabling prompts — only calls matching that specific rule are pre-approved; anything else still triggers the gate as usual. This is the intended workflow: if you find yourself approving the same command every day, promote the decision into a durable rule instead of re-answering the prompt. The finer point of exactly which settings file receives the rule comes later — the beginner takeaway is: 'always' means a rule was written.

question: You script claude -p "..." in a CI pipeline, and the run stops partway when the model proposes a command not covered by any rule. Why, and what's the fix?
options: Headless runs have no human to answer permission prompts, so unmatched actions can't be interactively approved — configure the allowlist or a non-prompting permission mode up front
The -p flag disables all tools by default, so any tool call fails until you re-enable them with a flag

CI machines lack the per-user approval cache under ~/.claude where your interactive 'always allow' answers are stored, so you must run one interactive session on the runner first to warm it before headless runs will succeed
Bedrock-backed sessions require IAM approval for each new command pattern, so the pattern must be added to the role policy
explanation: The permission gate works identically in headless mode — what's missing is the fallback. Interactively, an unmatched tool call pauses the loop and asks you; with claude -p there is nobody to ask, so the run stops at the gate. Non-interactive runs therefore need their permission decisions made in advance: allow rules covering everything the task legitimately needs, or a permission mode that doesn't prompt (bypass-permissions being acceptable precisely in isolated CI environments, where the blast radius is bounded). The -p flag changes input/output behavior, not tool availability. Past approvals do persist — but as rules in settings files, which you can ship to CI; there's no separate 'approval cache' to warm up. And the IAM option is a category confusion: IAM governs whether your AWS credentials may call the Bedrock API at all, while tool permissions are local harness policy, identical on every provider.

question: File-edit approvals are drowning you in prompts, but you still want to personally approve every shell command. Which setup fits?
options: Bypass-permissions mode — it approves edits automatically while still prompting for Bash
Plan mode — it lets file edits through silently while keeping commands gated
Accept-edits mode — it auto-approves file edits while other actions, like commands, still go through the normal gate
Default mode plus an allow rule for Bash(*) — that removes the noisiest prompts
explanation: Accept-edits mode exists for exactly this asymmetry: file edits are the routine bulk of permission prompts, so the mode auto-approves them while leaving everything else — notably shell commands — under the normal ask behavior. The distractors each break one half of the requirement. Bypass-permissions doesn't discriminate: it skips prompting for everything, commands included, which is why it belongs only in isolated, disposable environments. Plan mode points the opposite way — it's the read-only mode, so edits aren't silently allowed, they're not allowed at all. And allowing Bash(*) is precisely backwards: it silences command prompts (the ones you wanted to keep) while doing nothing about edit prompts. The underlying model: modes shift where the prompting threshold sits without touching the rule machinery — accept-edits moves edits below the threshold and leaves commands above it.

question: A colleague says: 'Sandboxing is just another name for the allow/deny rules — one mechanism, two doc pages.' What's the correction?
options: Close — sandboxing is the deny list specifically, while 'permissions' properly refers to the allow and ask lists

They're different layers answering different questions: rules are harness policy on whether a tool call may run at all; the sandbox is OS-level containment on what a running command can touch — and they compose
Backwards — once sandboxing is enabled it replaces the rules entirely, because the operating system takes over policy from the harness

They're the same gate under two names: 'permissions' is the label for the interactive prompting surface, while 'sandboxing' is what the identical rule engine is called when it runs non-interactively — in CI pipelines or against Bedrock
explanation: Two layers, two questions. Permission rules sit at the harness's gate and decide 'may this tool call execute at all?' — policy, evaluated before anything runs. Sandboxing assumes the call runs and uses operating-system isolation primitives to bound what it can do: restricting filesystem writes outside the workspace and limiting network access. Because the layers are independent, they compose into defense in depth — a command the rules permit can still be unable to write outside the project, because the OS stops it underneath. That composition has a practical payoff: when the harness knows a command is confined, it can afford to prompt less, since even a bad command has a bounded blast radius — sandboxing reduces prompt fatigue rather than adding friction. Neither layer replaces the other, and neither is provider-specific: both run locally, identical on Bedrock and the Anthropic API.

question: You're in accept-edits mode, yet one particular file edit still got blocked. A colleague concludes the mode is broken. What's the more likely explanation?
options: A deny rule matched the action — modes only shift where the ask threshold sits; explicit rules still exist underneath, and a deny is enforced in every mode
Accept-edits mode only covers files that existed when the session started; edits that create new files always go through the full gate
The mode silently reset — modes are per-turn state, and a system-reminder switched the session back to default between your turns
The file's content sat in the cached region of the prompt, and cached content can't be modified until the cache entry expires
explanation: Modes and rules are different instruments on the same gate. A mode is a session-level dial over the ask behavior — accept-edits moves routine edits below the prompting threshold. Rules are durable configuration underneath, and they resolve deny-wins: a deny from any settings tier blocks the matching call outright, in any mode. So a blocked edit under accept-edits usually means a deny rule (perhaps from the project or a managed tier) matched that path — the mode was never in a position to override it, because modes adjust asking, not deny enforcement. The distractors misapply real mechanisms: there's no existing-files-only carve-out; system-reminders inform the model about state, they don't flip permission modes between turns; and the prompt cache lives server-side as attention state over request bytes — it has no connection to whether a local file may be edited.

question: A colleague answers a permission prompt with 'always allow' and claims: 'That just set an in-memory flag in the harness — nothing on disk changed.' What actually happened, and where?
options: A rule was appended to the project's shared .claude/settings.json — the tier permission prompts always write to — so the whole team inherits the approval on their next git pull, which is why teams review that file in PRs
The colleague is right — 'always' persists only for the running session and is forgotten when it ends
A durable allow rule was appended to a settings file — typically the project's .claude/settings.local.json, which stays out of version control — making the approval personal and permanent
A rule was appended to ~/.claude/settings.json, making the approval global across every project on the machine
explanation: 'Always' is rule-writing, and where the rule lands is the load-bearing detail. The harness appends it to a settings file — typically the project's settings.local.json, the tier designed to be personal and gitignored. That placement threads two needles: the approval is durable (unlike a session-scoped answer, which is what the prompt's 'for this session' option gives you), yet it's scoped to you and this project. The near-miss tiers are wrong in instructive ways: writing to the shared project settings.json would silently push your personal approval onto every teammate through version control, and writing to the user-level file would apply it to every project on your machine — both broader than what you consented to at the prompt. Because the rule is just a settings entry, you can inspect it, edit it, or deliberately promote it to a shared tier later — the prompt simply automated the first write.

question: You run /compact focus on the database schema decisions — with that trailing text after the command. What does it do?
options: Filters the transcript on disk so only the database-related messages are retained
Restricts the fold to messages mentioning the database, leaving all other turns untouched in context
Sets a persistent session topic that every future auto-compaction will also follow
Runs a normal compaction, but passes your text as guidance so the summary emphasizes and preserves that content
explanation: /compact accepts focus instructions: the fold proceeds as usual — older history is summarized, recent exchanges kept — but your trailing text steers the summarizer toward what to preserve, so the schema decisions survive in the summary rather than being averaged away with everything else. The distractors misplace the effect. It's not a disk operation: the durable transcript is append-only and compaction only ever appends to it (summary plus boundary marker). It's not selective folding: the fold still covers the older history as a whole; your text shapes the summary's emphasis, not which messages get folded. And it's one-shot guidance for this fold, not persistent state — if you want standing guidance that every compaction honors, the documented lever is a 'when summarizing, preserve…' note in CLAUDE.md, which the compactor reads each time it runs.

question: In a typical coding session, which contributor tends to fill the context window fastest — and therefore brings auto-compaction closer?
options: Your own prompts, since user messages are kept at higher fidelity than other content
Tool outputs — file reads, search results, command output — which the loop appends in full and then resends every turn
The system prompt, which the harness grows a little on every turn to track session state
The model's replies, and extended thinking especially — output tokens count double against the window, so verbose reasoning fills it fastest
explanation: Context grows with everything the loop appends — prompts, replies, tool inputs — but the big one is tool outputs. A single file read can add thousands of tokens; a broad search or verbose test run, more; and because the stateless loop resends the whole conversation each turn, every one of those tokens is carried forward on every subsequent call. That's why exploration-heavy sessions hit auto-compaction far sooner than chat-heavy ones. The distractors miss the accounting: user prompts are usually tiny by comparison and nothing is stored at 'higher fidelity'; the system prompt is a stable, re-injected layer, not an accumulating one; and everything in the assembled request counts against the window, not just replies. The practical lever follows directly: push heavy exploration into subagents, whose tool outputs stay in a separate loop and return only a summary — keeping the parent's window lean and the fold further away. And no token counts double against the window — thinking or not, each token occupies exactly one slot.

question: What actually causes auto-compaction to trigger in a session?
options: The assembled context approaching the model's window limit
The session passing a fixed number of conversation turns
The transcript file on disk exceeding a size threshold
A timer — sessions compact automatically after a period of inactivity
explanation: Auto-compaction is window-pressure driven: as the context that would be assembled into the next request nears the model's finite window, the harness folds older history into a summary so the session can continue. (The exact trigger threshold is deliberately undocumented — what's documented is the mechanism, not the number.) The wrong options each measure the wrong thing. Turn count is uncorrelated with size: ten turns of file reads can outweigh a hundred turns of chat. Disk size is the wrong tier entirely — compaction manages the reconstructed context sent in requests, while the durable transcript is append-only and never the constraint. And there's no idle timer; an untouched session consumes no window. Since the window is a property of the model and compaction is harness logic, the behavior is identical against Bedrock and the Anthropic API — same weights, same window, same fold.

question: To check whether compaction has ever run, a colleague greps their transcript .jsonl files for 'compact_boundary', gets several hits, and declares proof. What's the flaw?
options: There is none — that string only ever appears inside genuine boundary records, so any hit is proof
The flaw is the tool: transcript files are stored in a binary encoding, so grep cannot see real records at all

Grep matches substrings, not records: a conversation that merely discussed compaction contains the word in message text — you must parse structurally and check for a system record with subtype compact_boundary

The flaw is the location: boundary markers live in a separate per-session index file the harness keeps alongside the transcript, so any hit inside the .jsonl itself can only be quoted message text rather than a real boundary record
explanation: A real fold leaves a structural artifact: a record with type "system" and subtype "compact_boundary" appended to the transcript. But grep finds substrings anywhere — and a session where you talked about compaction (reading docs, writing a quiz about it) contains the literal string inside ordinary message text, with no boundary record behind it. The two are indistinguishable to grep and trivially distinguishable to a parser that checks the record's type and subtype fields. So hits alone prove only mention, not event. The other options fail on facts: transcripts are plain JSONL, perfectly greppable — that's exactly why the false positive is easy to hit; and the boundary marker does live in the transcript stream, not a side index. The transferable habit: when a grep looks like evidence about structured logs, confirm it's a record, not a mention, before building a conclusion on it.

question: You keep a running task list inside the conversation and want it to survive every auto-compaction. Which lever is actually documented to influence what the fold preserves?
options: A PreCompact hook that receives the summarizer's draft on stdin and can rewrite it before the fold is appended — its trigger field says whether the fold was manual or auto
Pinning the task-list messages with a /pin command, which the compactor must carry verbatim
Setting a compaction ratio in settings.json so that less of the history is dropped per fold
Adding a 'when compacting, always preserve the current task list' note to CLAUDE.md — the compactor reads your memory files and follows that guidance
explanation: The compactor reads the conversation including your CLAUDE.md when producing its summary, and a free-form 'when summarizing, preserve…' section is the documented way to steer every fold — it matches on intent, so the task list gets carried into each summary. For a one-off fold you can also pass focus text to /compact directly. The distractors are near-misses worth separating. PreCompact is real, but it's an observation seam: it fires before the fold with a trigger field of manual or auto, giving you a chance to archive state — it isn't an editor for the summarizer's output. There is no /pin command, and no documented ratio setting — the fold's thresholds are explicitly undocumented. The stronger move for anything that must always hold: put it in CLAUDE.md as content, since that layer is re-injected into every request and survives every fold by construction, guidance or no guidance.

question: A session auto-compacted yesterday; today you --resume it. What conversation state does the model see on your first new turn?
options: The full pre-fold history — resume replays the append-only transcript record by record, and since compaction never erases anything from disk, every original message is still there to be rebuilt into context
The post-fold working set — the summary plus the recent tail — because the fold's summary and boundary marker are durable records, and reconstruction honors them instead of replaying the folded turns
Only the summary — resume drops the recent tail as well, to be conservative about the window
A freshly re-summarized version — resume always re-runs compaction over the whole transcript before continuing
explanation: Keep the two tiers separate. The durable transcript really does still contain every pre-fold message — compaction is append-only on disk — and that's precisely the expert trap in the first option: true premise, wrong conclusion. Resume is a reconstruction, not a raw replay: the harness rebuilds the working state the session left behind, and because the fold appended its summary and a compact_boundary marker as durable records, reconstruction assembles the post-fold state — summary standing in for the folded turns, recent tail intact. The boundary marker is what tells the assembler where the fold sits. This is exactly why the summary is persisted at all: so a resumed session continues from where compaction left it rather than resurrecting the oversized pre-fold context. No new summarization pass runs on resume, and the tail isn't dropped — resume neither redoes nor deepens the fold; it honors it.

question: Why is letting auto-compact fire in the middle of a complex task considered the worst timing, compared with running /compact yourself at a natural boundary?
options: Mid-task, the details you still need are exactly the 'older history' at risk of being folded, and you forgo the control a manual compact gives you — timing and focus instructions; at a boundary, what's summarized away is finished work
Auto-compact uses a smaller, cheaper summarizer model than /compact does, so its summaries are systematically lower quality

Auto-compact fires from inside the loop between tool calls, where hooks cannot run — so it skips PreCompact entirely and a mid-task fold can never be archived first, whereas manual /compact runs from the prompt line where hooks are live and always fire
Mid-task folds risk corrupting the transcript's record ordering on disk, which manual compaction is designed to avoid
explanation: The fold mechanism is identical either way — same summarizer, same lossiness. What differs is what the loss lands on. Compaction is documented to be lossy about earlier conversation content, and mid-task, 'earlier content' includes constraints, decisions, and partial results your current work still depends on; a fold at that moment can quietly remove exactly what you need next. At a natural boundary, the foldable material is completed work whose summary suffices. Manual /compact adds two controls auto-compact can't: you pick the moment, and you can pass focus instructions to steer what the summary keeps. The distractors invent differences that don't exist: no separate cheaper summarizer model is documented, PreCompact fires for both paths — its trigger field distinguishing 'manual' from 'auto' exists precisely because both invoke it — and the transcript is append-only, never at risk of corruption from a fold. Compacting deliberately is context hygiene; compacting by accident is context roulette.

question: A colleague adopts a habit of running /compact every ten turns: 'a small context means cheap turns, so compacting constantly minimizes total cost.' What's wrong with the math?
options: Nothing — on the 1-hour cache TTL, prefix rewrites are free, so frequent folds cost only the summary's output tokens
Compaction's price is per-session, not per-fold: after the first expensive fold, later folds reuse the same summary at no extra model cost

Each fold pays a full-price read of the whole conversation plus a fresh cache write of the rewritten prefix, and abandons cheap ~0.1x cache reads — frequent small folds repeat those costs for little size relief, and every pass loses detail

It's correct against the Anthropic API but backwards on Bedrock, where cache writes are the discounted operation and reads carry the premium — AWS prices for storage rather than retrieval, so frequent small folds actually get cheaper there, not costlier
explanation: Compaction has a real per-fold price, and it's the same price whether the fold was needed or not: the summarization pass must read essentially the entire conversation at full input rates (little of it is cacheable), and the rewritten prefix abandons the existing cache, so the next request pays a cache write at a premium (1.25x base input at the 5-minute TTL) instead of ~0.1x reads. That trade is favorable when the folded bulk is large and many turns remain; folding every ten turns pays the fixed costs repeatedly for marginal size relief — and stacks lossiness, since each summary is a summary of a summary. The traps: 1-hour-TTL writes are more expensive than 5-minute writes (2x base), not free; there's no per-session amortization — every fold is its own model call; and Bedrock doesn't invert cache economics — writes carry the premium and reads the discount on both providers.

question: The compaction pass must re-read the entire conversation to write its summary — yet your session's long prefix is already sitting in the prompt cache. Why is that pass billed as an expensive full read rather than cheap cache reads?
options: Because the harness applies the fold first and summarizes second: by the time the summarizer reads the conversation, the prefix has already been rewritten around the compact_boundary marker, so nothing left in the cache matches the bytes it is handed
Because prompt caches are scoped to a single conversation thread, and the compactor runs as a separate thread under its own cache namespace
Because the harness deliberately bypasses the cache for summarization, to guarantee the summary isn't produced from stale cached content

Because caching matches byte-identical prefixes from position zero, and the summarization request is assembled differently from the session's ordinary requests — little of it lines up with the cached prefix, so the read bills at full input price
explanation: Cache hits require the new request to reproduce the cached bytes exactly, from the very start. The session's cache entries correspond to the session's own assembly — its system prompt, tool schemas, then history. The summarization call is a differently shaped request: the same history wrapped in different instructions and structure, so the byte-for-byte prefix match fails early and the bulk of the read bills at full input price. That's why the fold's first cost is one full pass over everything being folded. The first option is an order trap: the summary is produced before the fold exists — the prefix rewrite is a consequence of the summarization, not something that precedes its read. The others invent mechanisms: caches aren't namespaced per conversation thread (any request reproducing the prefix can hit), and there's no staleness bypass — the cache stores attention state over exact bytes, so 'stale content' isn't a failure mode that needs dodging.

question: Mid-session, you run /model and switch to a different Claude model. What happens?
options: The session restarts with fresh context, because a conversation is bound to the model that started it

The very next API call goes to the new model carrying the entire existing conversation — model choice is just a field the harness sets per request, and the resend delivers full history to whichever model receives it
The switch is queued until the next compaction, when the summary can be handed to the new model cleanly

New turns go to the new model, but tool_results answering calls the old model emitted still route back to it — the loop keeps each tool_use/tool_result pair on the model that opened it, for consistency of that exchange, before switching over fully
explanation: This is the stateless loop paying off as a prediction. There is no server-side conversation bound to any model — every turn, the harness reassembles the full request from scratch and stamps a model identifier on it. /model changes that per-request field, so the next call simply targets the new model, which reads the entire resent history exactly as any model does on any turn: for the first time. Nothing needs restarting, queuing, or migrating, and there's no split routing — the loop has one outbound call per iteration, and every part of it goes to the currently selected model. One cost caveat worth knowing: prompt caches are model-specific, so the first call after a switch typically misses the cache and pays a fresh write of the prefix on the new model. On Bedrock the mechanics are identical — you're just switching which model ID the harness puts on the request.

question: Mid-session, you add a new deny rule to your settings. When does it start biting, and what does the change cost in tokens?
options: It gates the very next matching tool call, and costs zero tokens — permission rules are consulted at each gate check and never enter the request payload
It takes effect at the next session, and costs zero tokens — settings files are snapshotted once when the session starts
It gates the next tool call, at the cost of a small system-reminder injection so the model knows to stop proposing the blocked command
It takes effect immediately, at the cost of a one-time cache rewrite, since permission rules hash into the request's stable prefix
explanation: Permissions sit on the per-turn side of the cadence line: the harness consults the rules at each gate check, when a tool_use actually arrives, so a rule added mid-session governs the very next matching call — no restart needed. And because permissions are harness-shaping configuration, they never cross the wire: zero tokens, zero cache effect, invisible to the model. The near-misses each borrow a real mechanism from an adjacent surface. Session-start snapshotting is true of the tool inventory and MCP connections, not of permission rules. System-reminders are a real channel, but enforcement doesn't depend on one — the harness blocks the call regardless, and the model discovers the boundary through the rejection that comes back as its tool_result. And nothing about rules is 'hashed into the prefix' — the request payload doesn't contain them, which is precisely why editing them is the free kind of mid-session change.

question: Mid-session, you drop a new skill directory into ~/.claude/skills. Can the model trigger that skill in this same session?
options: Yes, from the next turn — the assembler re-scans the skill directories at every request assembly and re-collects names and descriptions, the same way CLAUDE.md is re-read from disk and re-injected each turn
Yes, but only after the next compaction, which rebuilds the request's stable head with the new description included
Generally not — the skill and plugin inventory is established at session initialization, like the tool set, so a new skill becomes available in a new or restarted session
No, and not next session either, until the skill is also registered under enabledPlugins in settings.json
explanation: Mid-session-change questions always reduce to cadence: is the surface re-resolved per turn, or fixed at session start? Content layers like CLAUDE.md are re-read into every request — that's the per-turn side. But the loaded skill/plugin inventory is infrastructure for the loop, resolved when the session initializes alongside the tool schemas and MCP connections; the assembler doesn't re-scan skill directories every turn. So the new skill's description won't appear in this session's ambient layer, and the model can't trigger what it can't see — a new or restarted session picks it up. The first option is the classic near-miss: applying CLAUDE.md's per-turn cadence to a session-scoped surface. Compaction is irrelevant — it folds history, it doesn't re-run configuration resolution. And enabledPlugins governs plugins, not ordinary skill directories; no such registration gate applies here.

question: System-reminders are consistently injected near the tail of the message array rather than folded into the system prompt at the head. Why is that placement load-bearing?
options: Because models weight recent tokens most heavily, and reminders must outrank the system prompt to be reliably obeyed

Because the Messages API enforces strict user/assistant role alternation and rejects system-role content mid-array, so harness-authored state updates are only legal when embedded in the latest user-role message — which is necessarily at the tail
Because tail tokens are billed at cache-read rates while head tokens bill at full input price, making the tail the economical place to inject

Because caching matches from the start of the request: appending at the tail leaves the cached head byte-stable, while mutating the system layer would invalidate the prefix and force an expensive rewrite every time state changed
explanation: System-reminders exist to solve a genuine tension: the model is stateless, so fresh, volatile state must be delivered inside the request — but prompt caching only pays off if the request's head stays byte-identical turn over turn. Injecting near the tail resolves both: the reminder reaches the model, while everything ahead of it still matches the cached prefix, exactly like appending any new user message or tool result. Delivering the same information by editing the system layer would rewrite the stable head and abandon the cache on every state change — precisely the expensive class of mid-session edit. The traps: recency effects in attention are real but are not the documented design driver here — placement is a cache decision, not a psychology one. No role-alternation rule forces this; the harness shapes the message array freely. And the third option inverts the economics — the cached head is where the cheap ~0.1x reads happen; fresh tail tokens bill as new input.

question: A colleague declares: 'Any mid-session configuration change invalidates the prompt cache, so freeze all config the moment a long session starts.' What's the accurate cost picture?
options: Close — every surface except permissions invalidates the cache, because rules are the one piece of config the payload never carries, while all other edits rewrite the prefix

Wrong twice over: harness-only changes (rules, hooks, modes) never touch tokens or cache at all; tail-delivered updates cost their own tokens but preserve the cached head; only rewrites of the stable head — the CLAUDE.md layer, the tool set — abandon the prefix
Inverted — mid-session edits are free across the board, because the cache keys only on the system prompt, and none of these surfaces ever modify what that parameter contains

The invalidation claim holds, but the remedy is wrong: the cache re-forms on the very next turn at the discounted ~0.1x read rate rather than the write premium, so even constant config churn has its total cost bounded at one cheap re-read per edit — freezing config buys nothing measurable
explanation: Rank every mid-session edit by where it lands. Class one, harness-only: permission rules, hooks, mode switches — never transmitted, so zero tokens and zero cache effect; change these freely. Class two, tail-delivered: system-reminders, new messages, tool results — they cost their own tokens but append after the cached head, leaving the prefix intact. Class three, stable-head rewrites: editing content in the CLAUDE.md/system layer or changing the tool set perturbs the prefix, and the next request pays a fresh cache write (1.25x base at the 5-minute TTL) for everything after the edit point instead of ~0.1x reads. So 'freeze everything' overcorrects — only class three is priced, and even that is a one-time miss, often worth it when deliberate. The first option flips the exception into the rule; the third pretends class three away; the fourth gets the re-forming right but the arithmetic wrong — the recovery write is the premium operation, and repeated churn pays it repeatedly.

question: A skill triggers at turn 10 of a session, injecting its roughly 3,000-token body. What happens to that body over turns 11, 12, 13, and beyond?
options: It is now part of the conversation history, so the stateless loop resends it on every subsequent turn — billed (at cache-read rates once stable) until a compaction folds it or /clear drops it

The harness prunes it from the assembly once the skill's task completes — bodies are tagged as ephemeral content at injection, so the next rebuild drops them and the context returns to its pre-trigger size
It is resent only on turns where the model actively uses the skill; idle turns skip it to save tokens
It migrates into the stable head after one turn, joining the descriptions so that future triggers of the same skill are free
explanation: Skill bodies are loaded on demand, but they don't unload on their own. Once injected into the message flow, the body is conversation history like anything else — and the stateless loop resends the whole history every turn. So a 3,000-token body invoked at turn 10 is carried on turns 11, 12, 13... typically at cache-read rates once the prefix over it stabilizes, until a compaction folds it into a summary or /clear empties the context. The distractors each require machinery that doesn't exist. The harness has no notion of a skill's task 'completing,' and history isn't editable retroactively — content woven in stays in. Nor is assembly selective per turn: the request carries the accumulated conversation, not a per-turn curation of which past pieces seem relevant. And nothing promotes into the stable head — the ambient layer holds descriptions only; bodies always live in the foldable flow. Invoke heavyweight skills with this tail cost in mind.

question: Skills can trigger two ways: the model decides to use one, or you type its slash name. How do the two paths differ mechanically?
options: User-triggered skills run inside a subagent, while model-triggered ones run inline in the main loop
Model-triggered skills load only the body, while user-triggered ones also inject the description alongside it for grounding

Only the decision differs: model-triggering relies on the ambient description matching the task, while typing the name forces the load directly — after the trigger, both converge on the same mechanics of injecting the body and proceeding with it in context

User-triggered skills bypass the model's decision at the mechanical level too: the harness parses the slash name, executes the skill's instructions itself as a script, and injects only the finished output into the conversation as a tool_result for the model to build on
explanation: Two doors into one room. On the model-triggered path, the model surveys the ambient name-and-description layer, judges that the task matches a skill, and invokes it; on the user-triggered path, typing the slash name is the signal, and no description matching is involved at all — which is why an explicit invocation works even when a description is too vague for the model to ever pick the skill itself. From the trigger onward the paths are identical: the harness loads the body into the message flow, and the model proceeds with those instructions in context. The distractors invent asymmetries: whether a skill delegates to a subagent is a property of that skill's design, not of which door was used; descriptions are already ambient in every request regardless; and the harness never executes skill instructions itself — a skill body is content for the model to follow, not code for the harness to run.

question: Skills' progressive disclosure — descriptions always in context, bodies loaded only on trigger — has a close structural analog elsewhere in Claude Code. Which is it?
options: Hooks, which keep lightweight event names ambient in context and load their scripts only when an event fires

MCP deferred tool loading, where tool names ride along ambiently and full schemas are fetched only when needed — the same trade of a small permanent index deferring a large cost until proven necessary
Compaction, which keeps a summary ambient and reloads the full folded history whenever the model asks for it

Subagents, which keep a lightweight agent roster ambient in the parent's context and page each agent's full transcript into the parent's window on demand — the same trade of a small resident index against a large deferred payload
explanation: Both mechanisms resolve the same impossible trade-off with the same shape. The model can only use what it can discover, so some index must always be present — but shipping every full definition ambiently would devour the window. Skills split description (always) from body (on trigger); deferred MCP loading splits tool names (always) from full schemas (fetched on demand). Small permanent tax, large deferred cost — paid only when a capability is actually exercised. The distractors fail the pattern on one side or the other. Hooks have no ambient half at all: they're harness-side callbacks costing zero context, with nothing for the model to discover. Compaction is one-way: folded history is not reloadable on request — the summary replaces it. And subagent transcripts never page into the parent; isolation is the entire point, with only the final result returning by value. The recurring design lesson: context is the scarce resource, so indexes stay resident and payloads stay lazy.

question: A skill wraps a heavy forty-step procedure that generates large intermediate outputs. Its author designs it to delegate the work to a subagent rather than run inline. At the mechanism level, what does that buy?
options: The subagent inherits the parent's cached prefix — the harness assembles it with the same system prompt and tool schemas so the existing cache entries carry over — and every step of the procedure therefore bills at ~0.1x cache-read rates instead of as fresh input
The body never needs to be written at all — the subagent can derive the full procedure from the skill's ambient description alone
It makes the procedure durable: a subagent's context survives /clear and compaction, unlike skill bodies injected inline

The procedure — its instructions, tool calls, and verbose outputs — runs in a separate loop with its own context, and only the final result returns to the parent as a single tool_result; the parent's conversation never carries the bulk
explanation: This combines skill injection with context isolation. Run inline, the forty steps and their outputs would all enter the parent's history — resent every subsequent turn and dragging the session toward compaction. Delegated, the subagent runs a separate loop with its own system prompt, context window, and transcript; it sees none of the parent's history, does the heavy work there, and hands back only its final text as one tool_result. The parent's context grows by a summary, not a procedure. The traps each break a real boundary. A subagent doesn't inherit the parent's cached prefix — it's a differently assembled request, so the parent's cache entries don't apply to it. The body is still essential: it's what instructs the delegation and the work; descriptions are routing signals, far too thin to derive a procedure from. And durability is backwards — a subagent's context is discarded when it finishes; nothing about it outlives the parent's resets.

question: A colleague asserts: 'Once a skill has fired, its instructions govern the rest of the session — they're in context for good.' What's the correction?
options: The body lives in the foldable conversation history: a compaction can summarize it away and /clear drops it outright — only the ambient description is guaranteed present afterward, and recovering the full instructions means re-triggering the skill

The opposite problem is real — the harness ages injected bodies out of the assembly after a fixed turn budget to bound their tail cost, so a skill must be re-triggered even in short sessions that never compact or clear, which is why long procedures re-fire midway
Right about persistence but wrong about scope: a fired skill's body is promoted into the stable head, where it persists across sessions until the skill is uninstalled
Right for user-triggered invocations, but model-triggered bodies are released as soon as the model emits its next end-of-turn
explanation: The skill system's two tiers have two lifecycles, and the colleague has granted the body the description's durability. Descriptions live in the always-present ambient layer — re-injected into every request, surviving every fold, like CLAUDE.md. The body, once injected, is ordinary conversation history: the same foldable tier as your early prompts, subject to the documented lossiness of compaction and to /clear. After a fold, the summary may retain a trace of what the skill said, but the operative instructions can be gone — and if the session still needs them, the fix is to re-trigger the skill, which reloads the body fresh. The traps invent lifecycles that don't exist: no turn-count expiry, no promotion into the stable head (bodies never join the prefix — that's precisely why invoking a skill doesn't reset the cache), and no trigger-path dependence — how a body arrived has no bearing on how long it survives. Rules that must always hold belong in CLAUDE.md, not in a fired skill's body.
